result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.is_connected()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Check if graph is connected. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L11442-L11510){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.is_connected() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Is connected](/assets/graphs/is-connected.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Left: two triangles, A B C and D E F, joined by the edge between C and D, so every node can reach every other and is_connected() returns True. Right: the same graph without the C-D edge (drawn dashed in the accent color), which leaves two separate pieces, so is_connected() returns False." width="100%"} A graph is connected if there is a path between every pair of nodes, i.e. it consists of a single connected component. The check starts a traversal from one node and verifies that it reaches all others. For directed graphs, edge direction is ignored, so this tests *weak* connectivity: `A -> B <- C` counts as connected even though `A` cannot reach `C` by following arrows. Use `is_strongly_connected()` if direction matters. Connectivity is a precondition for many measures, so it's worth checking before you: - compute distance-based metrics (diameter, average path length, closeness), which are undefined or misleading across separate components - interpret a network as a single system rather than several independent pieces - test whether removing a node or edge splits the network apart If the graph is not connected, `count_weakly_connected_components()` tells you how many pieces there are. The check ignores the current selection. For directed graphs, the reverse-edge lookup scans the edge list for each visited node, so it can be noticeably slower than the undirected case on large graphs. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : `True` if every node can reach every other node, `False` if the graph has more than one component. An empty graph and a single-node graph both count as connected. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} A path `A -- B -- C` links every node to every other, so it's connected: ::: {#2bc641e6 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C")]) ) graph.is_connected() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` True ``` ::: ::: Adding a node with no edges gives it no path to the rest of the graph, breaking connectivity: ::: {#744810df .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.add_node(label="D") graph.is_connected() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` False ``` ::: ::: In a directed graph, direction is ignored. Both edges point into "B", so "A" can't reach "C" by following arrows, yet the graph still counts as (weakly) connected; the strong-connectivity check says otherwise: ::: {#6c69ab66 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} directed = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("C", "B")]) ) directed.is_connected(), directed.is_strongly_connected() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (True, False) ``` ::: :::
